hazards.block-eyewash-path: Those cases are stacked directly in front of the eyewash station. An eyewash that takes ten seconds to reach because of a delivery nobody moved yet is an eyewash that misses the one window that actually matters after a splash.
hazards.mix-incompatible-chemicals: You're about to pour that returned cleaner straight into the floral preservative bucket to save a trip to the shelf. Two chemicals with no checked compatibility do not get combined on a guess — the SDS for each one is what tells you whether that's a reaction waiting to happen, not how full the bucket looks.
hazards.skip-ppe-goggles: You're reaching for the concentrate with no eye protection on. The splash risk on a concentrate is exactly what OSHA 29 CFR 1910.133 rates eye protection for — the goggles go on before the cap comes off, not after something already went wrong.
hazards.unlabeled-bottle: That spray bottle has no label on it at all. A decanted chemical with nothing written on the bottle is a chemical nobody after you can identify — OSHA's hazard communication rule exists because the one thing worse than a hazardous chemical is one nobody can name in an emergency.

interrupts.alert: A coworker is about to pour a different floral chemical straight into your mixed preservative bucket to save a second trip to the shelf.
interrupts.cue: That's two chemicals about to combine with nobody having checked compatibility.
interrupts.missNote: The pour happened before anyone checked the chart. Whatever that combination does, nobody standing there actually knew it was safe before it happened — which is exactly what the chart was there to answer.
interrupts.why: Pointing them at the compatibility chart before that pour happens is the entire lesson this station teaches, handed to somebody else in real time — a shortcut that skips the chart is a shortcut that skips the one thing standing between a convenience and a reaction.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the compatibility chart — check it before that second chemical goes into the bucket.

interrupts.alert: Someone from another department is walking straight toward the spill area, unaware it's an active chemical cleanup.
interrupts.cue: Get them behind the barrier before they walk through it.
interrupts.missNote: They walked through the spill area before anyone redirected them. Whatever was in that spill, it's now on a second person's shoes, tracked toward wherever they were headed.
interrupts.why: A spill area with no barrier around it looks, to anyone who wasn't there when it happened, like an ordinary wet spot to step around — pointing them behind the barrier is what keeps a contained cleanup from becoming a second person's exposure.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the spill barrier — get them behind it before they walk through the area.

lateNotes.goggles: Not yet — these go on before the concentrate's cap does, not after.
lateNotes.preservative-meter: Not until the SDS and the compatibility chart are both checked. This gets mixed to the label, not from memory.

name: Pharmacy & Floral Chemical Handling and SDS

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Compare what's on the shelf against today's inventory list for both departments.
steps.prompt: Compare what's on the shelf against today's inventory list for both departments.
steps.title: Check the chemical inventory board
steps.why: The inventory board is the only record of what's actually supposed to be on these shelves — a chemical that shows up without a line on the board is one nobody has checked against an SDS yet, and that gets caught here, not after it's already stored.

steps.cue: Pull the safety data sheet for the chemical you're about to store or mix.
steps.prompt: Pull the safety data sheet for the chemical you're about to store or mix.
steps.title: Look up the SDS before handling anything
steps.why: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 puts the SDS at the centre of hazard communication for exactly this reason — it's the one document that tells you the storage, handling and first-aid facts for this specific chemical, checked before the container is opened, not guessed at from the label's front panel.

steps.cue: Pull on the chemical-resistant gloves, then the splash goggles — in that order.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Wrong order — gloves go on first, then the goggles, so your hands are already protected before they touch anything else.
steps.prompt: Pull on the chemical-resistant gloves, then the splash goggles — in that order.
steps.title: Glove and goggle up
steps.why: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 and 1910.133 rate each piece for a different part of the same splash — gloves first so your hands are already covered by the time you reach for the goggles, not the other way around.

steps.cue: Check the chart before shelving this chemical anywhere near what's already stored.
steps.prompt: Check the chart before shelving this chemical anywhere near what's already stored.
steps.title: Check the storage compatibility chart
steps.why: A compatibility chart is what turns "there's room on this shelf" into an actual answer about whether two chemicals belong near each other — an acid and a base sharing a shelf because there was space is exactly the gap this chart exists to close.

steps.cue: Move the container that failed the compatibility check to its own segregated shelf.

drag.missNote: Not on the segregated shelf — an incompatible container anywhere else is one more thing somebody has to remember not to shelve beside it.

steps.prompt: Move the container that failed the compatibility check to its own segregated shelf.
steps.title: Move the incompatible container
steps.why: A container that fails the compatibility chart doesn't get left where it is because moving it is inconvenient — it goes to the shelf built for exactly this, right away, not on the next slow afternoon.

steps.cue: Two things in this storage area are wrong. Find them by looking.

decoyNotes.clean-container: This container is sealed, labelled and dry. Leave it.

itemNames.faded-label: a container with a faded, unreadable label
itemNames.leaking-container: a container leaking at the cap

itemNotes.faded-label: This label has faded past the point of actually being readable. A container nobody can positively identify anymore is treated as unknown, not assumed to still be whatever it was originally labelled.
itemNotes.leaking-container: This container is leaking at the cap seal. A slow leak on a shelf is a chemical exposure with nobody's name on it yet — it gets contained and reported, not left for the next person to find by touching it.

steps.prompt: Two things in this storage area are wrong. Find them by looking.
steps.title: Walk the chemical storage before it's touched
steps.why: A chemical storage check isn't finished when the shelf looks organised — it's finished when every container on it is actually sound and actually identifiable. Two things left wrong here become the next clerk's exposure.

steps.cue: Meter the concentrate into the water and commit once the mix is at the label's own ratio.

gauge.label: PRESERVATIVE MIX
gauge.missNote: Off the label's own ratio — remix rather than eyeball it closer next time.

steps.prompt: Meter the concentrate into the water and commit once the mix is at the label's own ratio.
steps.title: Mix the floral preservative to the label
steps.why: The label's ratio is the only number this mix is measured against — too weak and the preservative does nothing for the flowers it's meant to protect, too strong and it's an unnecessary chemical exposure for whoever handles the buckets next.

steps.cue: Open the spill kit and apply the absorbent, holding it down for the SDS's own dwell guidance.
steps.holdBreakNote: Lifted the absorbent early. Hold it down for the SDS's own guidance — a fast lift leaves the spill underneath it, not gone.
steps.prompt: Open the spill kit and apply the absorbent, holding it down for the SDS's own dwell guidance.
steps.title: Apply the spill kit per the SDS
steps.why: The spill kit's absorbent only does its job over the dwell time the SDS actually calls for — lifting it early leaves exactly the residue underneath that the kit was supposed to take care of.

steps.cue: Sweep the absorbed residue toward the containment bag at a slow, controlled pace.
steps.holdBreakNote: Out of the controlled band — slow the sweep before residue goes past the containment area.
steps.prompt: Sweep the absorbed residue toward the containment bag at a slow, controlled pace.
steps.title: Sweep the residue at a controlled pace
steps.why: A fast sweep flings residue outward past the containment area you just set up — a slow, controlled pass keeps everything the spill kit already absorbed inside the area meant to hold it.

steps.cue: Check that the path to the eyewash is clear and the unit activates.
steps.prompt: Check that the path to the eyewash is clear and the unit activates.
steps.title: Confirm the eyewash is clear and functional
steps.why: An eyewash confirmed clear before a chemical is even opened is what makes the ten seconds after a real splash a routine flush instead of a search for a station nobody checked was working.

steps.cue: Turn the ventilation fan switch on before working with the concentrate, per the SDS's guidance.
steps.prompt: Turn the ventilation fan switch on before working with the concentrate, per the SDS's guidance.
steps.title: Turn on the back-room ventilation
steps.why: The SDS's own ventilation guidance exists because a concentrate's fumes build up fastest in exactly the small back room this work happens in — the fan runs before the container opens, not after somebody notices the air feels wrong.

steps.cue: Move the used spill kit materials to the hazardous waste container, not the regular trash.

drag.missNote: Not in the hazmat bin — spill waste doesn't go in with the regular trash.

steps.prompt: Move the used spill kit materials to the hazardous waste container, not the regular trash.
steps.title: Dispose of the spill materials properly
steps.why: Absorbent that just took up a chemical is not regular trash anymore — the SDS's own disposal guidance is what tells you it goes to a hazardous waste container, and skipping that step just relocates the exposure instead of ending it.

steps.cue: Fill out the incident form for the spill before the shift moves on.
steps.prompt: Fill out the incident form for the spill before the shift moves on.
steps.title: Log the spill
steps.why: A spill that isn't logged is a spill the next shift has no way of knowing happened — the form is what turns a cleaned-up mess into a record somebody can actually act on if it happens again.

steps.cue: Sign the log to close out today's chemical handling check.
steps.prompt: Sign the log to close out today's chemical handling check.
steps.title: Sign the chemical handling log
steps.why: The signature is the clerk taking responsibility for the whole check — every chemical inventoried, checked against its SDS, stored compatibly and any spill logged — and it's the record read if either department's chemical handling is ever questioned.

tagline: A chemical checked against its own SDS before it's stored, mixed to the label or cleaned up, with the eyewash proven clear and the incident logged
